sets.title: The Weighbridge
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an extract from an original short story set in the Western Australian wheatbelt. The town is fictional.
sets.body:
Every December my father drove the harvest to the bins at Wilgarup, and every December he took one of us with him for the weighing. That year it was my turn, though I was eleven and had begun, privately, to find him boring.

We left before the heat. The truck smelled of diesel and old oranges, and the wheat in the back hissed whenever we took a corner, as if the load were muttering about the road. My father drove with one wrist hooked over the wheel. He did not talk on these trips. He listened to the engine the way other men listened to the cricket, leaning slightly towards it, frowning at things I could not hear.

The queue at the bins was a mile of trucks, all of them painted the same tired colour by dust. Men stood beside their cabs in a loose line of hats and talked about rain that had not come and prices that had not gone up. My father nodded at them. Nobody said much. It was understood, I think, that whatever you had in the back of your truck was the whole of your year, and you did not discuss the whole of your year with a man who might have done better.

When it was our turn he eased the front wheels onto the weighbridge so gently that I felt the truck hesitate, the way a horse hesitates at water. Inside the little office a woman with reading glasses on a chain looked at a dial I could not see. Then she wrote a number on a docket and passed it through the window.

My father read it once. He folded the docket in half, and then in half again, until it was a small hard square, and he put it in the pocket of his shirt, over his heart, and buttoned the pocket.

'Good?' I said.

'It's a number,' he said.

On the way home he stopped at the roadhouse and bought me a lemonade and himself nothing. He sat on the bonnet in the heat with his hat tipped forward, looking at the paddocks we had passed that morning, which now looked exactly the same, stubble to the horizon, a few crows working the edges. I understood that he was doing a sum in his head and that I was not part of it.

It was years before I learned what that number meant: that it had been the worst harvest in a decade, that the bank had already written twice, that my mother had been up at night with the books spread over the kitchen table like a hand of cards that would not come right. Nobody told me. They protected me from it the way you protect a child from weather, by not mentioning it, by buying lemonade.

What I remember now is not the dial, which I never saw, or the number, which I never knew, but the way he buttoned the pocket. As if the year could be kept in there. As if folding a thing small enough made it possible to carry.

questions.model: The writer represents the farmers as a community bound by shared hardship but governed by a code of reticence and pride. Visually they are made indistinguishable: the trucks are "all of them painted the same tired colour by dust", a transferred epithet that gives the vehicles their owners' exhaustion and suggests that the drought has erased individual difference. The men themselves become "a loose line of hats", a synecdoche that reduces them to the outward sign of their work and keeps their faces, and feelings, out of view. Their conversation is built from negatives, "rain that had not come and prices that had not gone up", so that talk circles absence rather than naming anyone's loss. The adult narrator then makes the code explicit: "whatever you had in the back of your truck was the whole of your year". The weighty repetition of "the whole of your year" in the following clause shows why the men stay silent: each load is a private verdict on a year of labour, and comparing it risks humiliation. The community is therefore close yet guarded, sharing a hardship it will not openly discuss.

questions.model:
The passage presents silence largely as an act of care, but the retrospective narrator also exposes its cost: what protects the child also excludes them, and leaves the father carrying the year alone.

The clearest case for silence as care is the simile that the family protected the narrator "the way you protect a child from weather, by not mentioning it, by buying lemonade." Weather is something no one can control, so the comparison casts the failed harvest as a force the parents absorb on the child's behalf; the small, sweet detail of the lemonade becomes a gesture of love precisely because it replaces explanation. The father's terse reply, "It's a number," works similarly, its flat monosyllables refusing to let the docket's meaning reach the child.

Yet the passage is careful to show what this silence costs. On the bonnet the father is "doing a sum in his head", and the narrator recognises "that I was not part of it." The plain, final clause registers exclusion, not comfort. Silence also extends beyond the family: at the bins, the men's talk of "rain that had not come and prices that had not gone up" is a ritual of not saying, governed by an unwritten rule that "you did not discuss the whole of your year" with a man who might have done better. Here silence protects pride as much as people, suggesting that the father's reticence is partly learned stoicism rather than pure tenderness.

The ending holds both readings together. The adult narrator remembers "the way he buttoned the pocket", and the repeated "As if" fragments expose the wish behind the gesture: that "folding a thing small enough made it possible to carry." The conditional framing admits that the hope was an illusion; the debt did not shrink, it was simply carried privately. To a large extent, then, the passage presents silence as care, but as a care that isolates the carer, and the narrator's belated understanding becomes a quiet way of returning that care by finally naming what was unsaid.

sets.title: Sonnet for the Night Bus
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original poem. It is a Petrarchan sonnet: an eight-line octave followed by a six-line sestet.
sets.body:
The last bus out of Central keeps its time
for no one. Every window holds a screen,
a face lit blue above it: nurse in green,
two boys asleep in uniform, the grime
of somebody's whole shift along the line
of someone's sleeve. We do not speak. We lean
the way the bus leans, gently, as if we'd been
rehearsing this together all our lives.

Then, at the bridge, the harbour opens wide—
the whole black water stitched with lights—and one
by one we lift our heads, as if we'd heard
our names called out across it. No one tried
to say what we had seen. The bus moved on.
But for a moment we were all one word.

questions.model: The octave first presents the passengers as isolated individuals. Each is enclosed by technology, "Every window holds a screen, / a face lit blue above it", so the people appear as separate glowing units rather than a group, and the blunt short sentence "We do not speak" confirms their silence. Yet the poet undercuts this separation through movement: "We lean / the way the bus leans, gently". The enjambment across the line break makes the reader's voice lean forward with the passengers, and the shift to the collective pronoun "we" implies an unspoken, physical unity. The comparison "as if we'd been / rehearsing this together all our lives" suggests their shared motion is a kind of choreography, so strangers who never speak are still bound by a common rhythm.

questions.model: The final line suggests that the passengers' shared response to the harbour briefly fuses separate strangers into a single meaning. Its key metaphor, "we were all one word", is surprising because the octave stressed silence: "We do not speak", and later "No one tried / to say what we had seen." The irony is that the passengers become "one word" precisely when nobody speaks; their unity lies in a shared perception rather than in conversation. The image is prepared by the sestet's turn, when "one / by one we lift our heads, as if we'd heard / our names called out across it." The enjambment that splits "one / by one" enacts the gradual spread of attention from person to person, and the idea of hearing "our names" implies each passenger is individually recognised before they become collectively one. The opening conjunction "But" and the qualifier "for a moment" hold this unity in tension with the preceding sentence, "The bus moved on." The line therefore celebrates connection while conceding its brevity, leaving the reader with a moment of transcendence that is real yet temporary.

questions.model:
The poet uses the sonnet form highly effectively, because its compression, its turn and its rhyme all mirror the poem's subject: a connection that is ordered, intense and brief.

The Petrarchan structure divides the experience in two. The octave is enclosed and inward-looking, its images of "a face lit blue" and "the grime / of somebody's whole shift" confining the passengers to tired, private worlds. The volta at line 9, signalled by "Then, at the bridge, the harbour opens wide", physically opens the poem as the view opens, so the form's traditional shift of thought becomes a literal shift of vision. This is a purposeful use of convention rather than mere decoration.

Rhyme also works for meaning. Several rhymes are slant rather than full, such as "time" and "lives", or "one" and "on", so the sounds nearly but not quite match, like strangers who share a space without fully meeting. By contrast, the final rhyme, "heard" and "word", is a full rhyme, and it lands on the moment of unity, giving the closure a satisfying sense of completion.

The sonnet's brevity is perhaps its most effective feature. Fourteen lines leave no room for the connection to be explained or prolonged, and the poem refuses to prolong it: "The bus moved on." The plain monosyllables of that sentence return us to motion, so the final line's "for a moment" feels earned rather than sentimental. A longer free-verse form might have dwelt on the harbour; the sonnet instead frames the experience as tightly as memory does. Overall, the form does not merely contain the moment but enacts its fleetingness.

sets.title: What the Map Leaves Out
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original speech. The speaker, Dr Rania Saab, a paramedic, is fictional. She is addressing the graduating Year 12 students at the western Sydney high school she once attended.
sets.body:
Thank you, Mr Nguyen. Thank you, parents, grandparents, and the little brother in the third row who has clearly been promised something if he sits still.

Twenty years ago I sat where you are sitting, in a polyester gown that smelled of the storeroom, and I listened to a man in a very good suit tell us that the world was our oyster. I remember thinking two things. The first was that I had never eaten an oyster. The second was that if the world was an oyster, someone had already been told where the pearls were, and it was not us.

I am not here to tell you the world is your oyster. I am here to tell you about maps.

In my first year on the road as a paramedic, I was sent to a call in a street I had driven past a hundred times. The address was on the screen. The map was on the screen. The map said turn left. The map did not say that the left turn had been closed for roadworks for three weeks, or that the house numbers jumped from 14 to 40 because of a subdivision nobody had bothered to tell the council about, or that the woman we were looking for would be on the footpath in her dressing-gown, waving a tea towel so we could find her.

We found her because a boy on a bike, maybe ten years old, pedalled in front of the ambulance shouting, 'This way! This way!' He knew the street. He knew it because he lived in it. No satellite has ever known a street the way a ten-year-old on a bike knows it.

I have thought about that boy for twenty years.

Here is what he taught me. A map is a promise made by people who have never been where you are going. It is useful. Use it. But do not mistake it for the place. Some of you have been handed maps already: by your marks, by your postcode, by what people expect of a kid from here. Some of those maps will say turn left. Some of them will say there is nothing down this road worth seeing. Some of them will say, kindly, in a very good suit, that the pearls are elsewhere.

They are wrong about this suburb. I know because I have driven every street of it at three in the morning with the sirens off, and I have been let into kitchens where grandmothers who spoke no English made me eat before I could leave. I have seen teenagers do CPR on their fathers because a teacher in this hall made them practise on a dummy in Year 9. I have seen people who were told they would amount to nothing hold this place together with their bare hands.

So do not wait for someone to tell you where the pearls are. Be the boy on the bike. Know your street. Know it so well that when the map fails, and it will fail, you are the one who can say: this way.

And when you have learned your way, come back and shout it to the next ambulance, the next new teacher, the next frightened kid in a polyester gown.

This way. This way. Congratulations, and thank you.

questions.model:
The speaker develops the map as an extended metaphor for the expectations imposed on young people, and she reshapes her audience's sense of the future by showing that such maps can be wrong and that local knowledge can be more reliable.

She grounds the metaphor in a concrete anecdote before making it abstract. The repetition in "The address was on the screen. The map was on the screen. The map said turn left" builds a rhythm of mechanical confidence, which the next sentence dismantles through anaphora: "The map did not say" introduces a long cumulative list of what the technology missed. The accumulation makes official knowledge seem thin beside lived reality.

The boy on the bike then embodies the alternative. His shouted "This way! This way!" gives a voice to local expertise, and the aphorism "No satellite has ever known a street the way a ten-year-old on a bike knows it" elevates the child above the most distant, powerful technology.

Only then does the speaker define the metaphor: "A map is a promise made by people who have never been where you are going." The definition is balanced, "It is useful. Use it", but its warning, "do not mistake it for the place", applies the image directly to the audience. The tricolon of maps handed out "by your marks, by your postcode, by what people expect of a kid from here" names the specific judgements these students face, moving from personal to social expectation.

By the conclusion the metaphor becomes a call to action, "Be the boy on the bike", so the audience is repositioned from people who follow maps to people who can correct them.

questions.model:
The speech's structure is highly effective because it is circular and cumulative: it begins with a borrowed cliché, replaces it with a story the audience can own, and ends by handing that story back to them as a responsibility.

The opening uses humour to win a ceremonial audience. Thanking "the little brother in the third row" acknowledges the families present and relaxes the formality, while the recollection of "a man in a very good suit" announcing that "the world was our oyster" introduces the cliché she will dismantle. Her two thoughts, that she "had never eaten an oyster" and that "someone had already been told where the pearls were", turn the joke into a pointed critique of privilege. The short sentence "I am here to tell you about maps" then pivots the speech decisively, signalling a new, more honest frame.

The middle section is built as anecdote, then lesson, then application. Placing the paramedic story before any explicit message is persuasive because the audience experiences the map's failure before being told what it means; the one-line paragraph "I have thought about that boy for twenty years" marks the story's weight and slows the pace for reflection.

The speech then returns to its opening images, which gives the structure its power. The cliché resurfaces when maps "will say, kindly, in a very good suit, that the pearls are elsewhere", and the speaker rebuts it with the blunt "They are wrong about this suburb." Her evidence is local and emotive: grandmothers who "made me eat before I could leave" and teenagers doing CPR because "a teacher in this hall" made them practise. The deictic "this hall" ties abstract hope to the very room the audience sits in.

Finally, the structure closes the circle. The "frightened kid in a polyester gown" recalls the speaker's younger self, and the repeated "This way. This way." reclaims the boy's words as a collective motto. Ending on this echo is effective because the audience leaves not with the speaker's achievement but with their own instructions. The speech's one possible weakness is that its optimism rests on anecdote rather than broader evidence, but for a graduation audience that needs belief more than data, the structure is precisely judged.

sets.title: The Year of the Broken Arm
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original piece of memoir-style writing. The narrator and her family are fictional.
sets.body:
My sister broke her arm in the summer of 1998, and for twenty-five years we have disagreed about whose fault it was.

In my version, which I have told at three weddings and one funeral, we are at our grandparents' place in Mildura, and the fig tree in the backyard is the size of a house. Ellie is nine and I am eleven. She wants to climb to the high fork, where the figs are, because the birds have already got all the low ones. I tell her not to. I say it clearly, in an older-sister voice I have been practising, and then I go inside to watch the cricket with Pop. A minute later there is a sound like a stick snapping under a boot, and then nothing, and then Ellie screaming in a way I had not known a person could scream.

In Ellie's version, I dared her.

She is very calm about this. She says it the way you would say the date. 'You said I was too chicken to get to the fork,' she says. 'You said it twice. And then you went inside because you didn't want to watch me do it.' She says this at Christmas, over the pavlova, and my mother looks at the ceiling, and my partner looks at me with the interest of someone watching a documentary.

The difficulty is that I can see her version. I can see it quite clearly, which is the problem. I can see myself at the foot of the tree with my arms folded, and I can hear my voice saying chicken, and I don't know whether this is a memory or whether I have simply heard her story so many times that it has grown its own pictures, the way a room you have only heard described begins, after a while, to have furniture.

Memory, I have read, is not a recording but a performance. Each time we remember something we rebuild it from parts, and each time the parts are slightly different, like a cover band that has played the same song so often it has forgotten the original. This is meant to be comforting. It is not comforting. It means that somewhere in my head there is an eleven-year-old who either told her sister to be careful or told her to be brave, and I cannot get her to tell me which.

What neither of us disputes is the hospital. The fluorescent light, the plaster going on white and warm, the nurse who let Ellie choose the colour of the cast, and the way she chose purple, then looked at me, and said I could be the first to sign it. I wrote my name so small that it disappeared under everyone else's by the end of the week.

I have been thinking about why I did that. It is possible I was being modest. It is possible I was ashamed. It is possible that even then, at eleven, I was already beginning to revise.

questions.model:
The writer deliberately withholds a verdict, but she shapes the reader's judgement so that Ellie's version gradually seems more credible, and the narrator's honesty about this becomes the passage's real subject.

At first the narrator's version is presented with confident, cinematic detail: the fig tree "the size of a house" and the precise sound "like a stick snapping under a boot". Yet she undercuts her own authority by admitting she has told it "at three weddings and one funeral", which suggests a polished performance rather than raw recall.

Ellie's version, by contrast, gains credibility through tone and specificity. She is "very calm about this" and says it "the way you would say the date", a simile that equates her claim with plain fact. Her quoted speech includes the exact taunt and the detail "You said it twice", and the motive she attributes to her sister, that she "didn't want to watch", is uncomfortably plausible.

Her analogy of a described room that begins "to have furniture" shows how retelling can manufacture images, which weakens both versions but especially her own, since it is her memory being reshaped. The image of memory as "a cover band" that "has forgotten the original" generalises the problem, so the reader judges the issue not as lying but as the ordinary instability of memory.

sets.title: Unexpected Item in the Bagging Area
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original opinion column written in the style of a regional newspaper. The columnist, Margaret Ellery, and the supermarket are fictional.
sets.body:
The new self-checkouts arrived at our supermarket on a Tuesday, which seems fitting. Nothing good has ever started on a Tuesday.

There are six of them now where Lorraine's register used to be. They are very clean. They speak in the voice of a woman who has never had a bad day in her life, and they want me to know, several times per transaction, that there is an unexpected item in the bagging area.

I want to be fair to the machines. They are fast, mostly. They do not take smoko. They do not, as far as I know, go home to a sick husband and come back the next morning with their lipstick on anyway. The company says they 'free up staff for customer service', and I'm sure somebody in a head office believes that, in the same way I am sure somebody believes the twelve-items-or-fewer sign is a law of nature.

But I have been shopping at that supermarket for thirty-one years, and here is what Lorraine knew that the machine does not. She knew that my mother had died, because she asked after her every Thursday for nine years and then one Thursday I could not answer, and she reached across the conveyor belt and held my wrist for a second, and then she scanned my teabags. She knew that the young bloke from the mechanic's buys the same pie every day and that if he didn't come in, someone should ring the garage. She knew which of the old men only came in to talk.

I don't have a graph to show you. I can't tell you what Lorraine was worth in dollars. That is rather my point. The things that hold a small town together don't show up on the spreadsheet, and so the spreadsheet concludes, quite reasonably, that they do not exist.

Some readers will say I am being sentimental. Fair enough. I am a sixty-four-year-old woman writing a column about a cash register; sentiment is my natural habitat. Others will say that progress is progress, and that people complained about the automatic car wash too. They did. They were right about that as well: there is nobody left at the car wash either.

So here is my modest proposal. Keep the machines, if you must. But keep one lane with a person in it. Call it the slow lane. Put a sign on it: For people who would like to be known. I suspect the queue will surprise you.

In the meantime, I have started going through the self-checkout with a single lemon, every day, just to keep the machine company. It thanks me for shopping with it. I tell it that's all right, love. Neither of us is fooled. But one of us, at least, is trying.

She mocks the self-checkouts' artificial cheer by describing their voice as that of "a woman who has never had a bad day in her life", contrasting the machine with the human worker whose loss she will lament. Yet she also says "I want to be fair to the machines" and concedes they are "fast, mostly", which presents her as reasonable rather than simply nostalgic. This balance of humour and fairness builds the trust she needs before making her emotional case about Lorraine.

She first addresses the company's claim that the machines "free up staff for customer service", undermining it through a sarcastic comparison with people who believe "the twelve-items-or-fewer sign is a law of nature", which implies the claim is a convenient corporate fiction. Later she names the charge her critics are most likely to make: "Some readers will say I am being sentimental." questions.model:
The column is highly persuasive for a sceptical reader because it never asks that reader to reject efficiency outright; instead it uses a disarming persona, a single powerful anecdote and a modest, practical proposal to shift attention from what machines do well to what they cannot measure.

A reader who favours self-checkouts is likely to be disarmed by the writer's fairness. She grants that the machines "are fast, mostly" and "do not take smoko", and her humour is aimed at corporate language rather than at people who like technology. Because she concedes ground early, her later criticism seems balanced rather than reactionary.

The anecdote about Lorraine is the column's emotional centre and its strongest evidence. The narration that Lorraine "reached across the conveyor belt and held my wrist for a second, and then she scanned my teabags" is persuasive precisely because of its understatement: the return to the ordinary task after the gesture of comfort shows care built into routine work. The anaphora of "She knew" then broadens the example from personal grief to community welfare, including the warning that "someone should ring the garage", which reframes a cashier as an informal safety net. A sceptic may dismiss nostalgia, but it is harder to dismiss the claim that a town loses this kind of attention.

The writer then turns the lack of data into an argument: "The things that hold a small town together don't show up on the spreadsheet". The irony of the spreadsheet concluding "quite reasonably" that such things "do not exist" exposes a limitation in the opposing logic rather than attacking its supporters.

Finally, the proposal is small enough to accept: "keep one lane with a person in it." The sign "For people who would like to be known" is memorable because it names a need most readers share. The closing image of buying "a single lemon" to keep the machine company is comic but poignant, and the last line, "But one of us, at least, is trying", gently implicates the reader in the choice. The column's reliance on one anecdote is a limitation, yet its persona and proposal make it difficult for even a committed sceptic to dismiss.

sets.title: The Interpreter
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an extract from an original short story; Text 2 is an original poem. Both are about language and family across generations.
sets.body:
The doctor talks to me, not to my father. This is the first thing I notice, and I am fourteen, so I notice it with a kind of pleasure.

'Ask him whether the pain is sharp or dull,' she says. 'Ask him how long.'

I turn to my father. He is sitting very straight on the plastic chair, his good jacket buttoned, his hands on his knees the way he sits in the photographs from before. I ask him in Vietnamese, and I make the question gentler on the way through, because the doctor's English is quick and flat and my father's ears go red when people are quick with him.

'Since Tết,' he says. 'It is nothing. Tell her it is nothing.'

'Since about February,' I tell the doctor. 'He says it's sharp sometimes.'

He did not say that. But I have heard him at night, the small sound he makes turning over, and I think the doctor should know. My father watches my mouth while I speak, trying to catch the shape of his own words in it. I watch him watching me. Between us there is a little bridge made of my voice, and I am the only one who can walk across it.

The doctor writes something. She asks about his work, the lifting, the hours. I translate warehouse and night shift and twenty-two years. I do not translate the part where he says, 'Tell her I have never missed a day,' because the doctor has already looked at the clock, and because I know it would sound, in English, like a man asking for a medal.

On the way out the receptionist says something about a referral, and my father nods as if he understands, and thanks her twice in his careful English, and I see her smile at him the way people smile at children who have said a new word. I want to tell her he was an engineer once. I want to tell her he can recite poems I will never be able to read. Instead I take the paper from her and fold it into my school bag.

In the car he says, 'What did you tell her?'

'Everything,' I say.

He starts the engine and does not look at me, and I understand that he knows I am lying, and that he is grateful, and that both of these things are true at once, the way it is both day and night somewhere at every minute.

pair.title: Mother Tongue
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
My grandmother kept her language in a tin
with the buttons and the rubber bands,
and when I was small she would open it for me:
words like boiled sweets, sharp at the edges,
that she placed on my tongue and told me not to swallow.

I swallowed them. I was a child.
I swallowed the word for the blue hour after rain
and the word for the cousin who does not visit
and the word for the ache you get from loving a place
that is not where you are.

Now she is ninety and the tin is empty,
or I have lost the key, or there was never a key,
only her hands, which were the key.
On the phone she says a sentence and waits.
I say, Yes, Nonna. I say, Me too.
I say the three words I still own
as if they were the whole of the house.

Somewhere inside me is a room
where all those swallowed words are still dissolving,
sweetening something I can't name.
I go there sometimes. I don't turn on the light.

She softens the doctor's questions, making them "gentler on the way through", because her father's ears "go red when people are quick with him", showing her sensitivity to his humiliation. She also adds information he withholds, telling the doctor the pain is "sharp sometimes" because she has heard "the small sound he makes turning over" at night, putting his wellbeing ahead of his stoic "It is nothing." Finally, she omits his claim that he has "never missed a day", fearing it would sound "like a man asking for a medal". questions.model: Text 2 represents the speaker's loss as gradual, partly self-inflicted and ultimately internalised. The extended metaphor of a language kept "in a tin / with the buttons and the rubber bands" makes it domestic and precious but also fragile, a household treasure rather than a public possession. The simile of words "like boiled sweets, sharp at the edges" captures their sensory pleasure, yet the instruction "not to swallow" hints that a language must be held and used, not consumed. The blunt confession "I swallowed them. I was a child." uses short sentences to convey both guilt and self-forgiveness. In the third stanza, the tricolon of uncertainty, the tin is empty, "or I have lost the key, or there was never a key, / only her hands", shows the speaker realising that the language lived in her grandmother's presence and cannot be recovered without her. questions.model:
Both texts represent language as the medium through which love between generations is expressed, yet each shows that language can also separate the people it connects. Text 1 locates this tension in a public, practical setting where the child holds linguistic power, while Text 2 presents a private, inward loss in which the child has surrendered that power.

In Text 1, language connects through mediation. The metaphor of "a little bridge made of my voice" captures the narrator's role as the only link between her father and the doctor, but the bridge also isolates her: "I am the only one who can walk across it." Language is a barrier for the father, whose "careful English" earns the smile given to "children who have said a new word", a simile that exposes how English infantilises him. The narrator's silent wish to say "he was an engineer once" shows that what cannot be translated is his dignity.

Text 2 reverses the direction of loss. Here the older generation holds the richer language and the younger has let it go: "I swallowed them. I was a child." Whereas the narrator of Text 1 chooses what to leave out, the speaker of Text 2 has no choice left; on the phone she can only answer "Yes, Nonna" and "Me too", a minimal exchange in which love persists while meaning thins. The barrier is not a doctor's clock but time itself, figured in the tin that is now "empty".

Both texts nonetheless suggest that connection survives beyond words. In Text 1, the father "does not look at me", yet the narrator understands that he knows she is lying and is "grateful", an understanding captured in the analogy that "it is both day and night somewhere at every minute." In Text 2, the lost words are "still dissolving, / sweetening something I can't name", a metaphor that relocates language from speech to feeling. Through prose narrative and lyric metaphor respectively, the texts together suggest that between generations language is never simply a bridge or a wall, but both at once, and that love often lives in the silence where translation fails.

sets.title: Penalty
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original short scene written for performance. The characters are fictional.
sets.body:
A car parked outside a suburban soccer ground, late afternoon. DANNY (12) sits in the passenger seat in a muddy uniform, boots still on. His father, MARK (40s), is in the driver's seat. The engine is off. A trophy, not theirs, glints through the windscreen as another family walks past.

MARK: Seatbelt.

(DANNY doesn't move. MARK waits, then reaches across and does it up for him, the way he did when DANNY was small. DANNY lets him.)

MARK: You want the radio?

DANNY: No.

MARK: Right.

(Pause. MARK taps the steering wheel, two beats, stops.)

MARK: The keeper guessed right. That's all that was. Fifty-fifty. Professionals miss those.

DANNY: You said go left.

MARK: I said — (He stops.) I said if you're not sure, go left.

DANNY: I was sure. I was going to go right. Then I looked at you.

(Silence. Outside, someone toots a horn and cheers. MARK watches them in the rear-view mirror until they are gone.)

MARK: When I was your age, my dad came to one game. One. Under-thirteens, against Penrith. I scored twice and he left at half-time because the car was making a noise.

DANNY: You've told me.

MARK: Have I.

DANNY: Every time we lose.

(MARK almost laughs. It doesn't quite arrive.)

MARK: So I come to all of them. Every Saturday. I thought that was — I thought if I was there, you'd...

DANNY: I know.

MARK: Do you?

(DANNY looks at his boots. He starts unlacing one, slowly, very carefully, as if it matters.)

DANNY: Next time can you stand somewhere I can't see you?

(It lands. MARK sits with it. He takes his hands off the wheel and puts them in his lap.)

MARK: Yeah. (Beat.) Yeah, mate. I can do that.

DANNY: Not far. Just — behind the goal or something. Where the other dads are.

MARK: Behind the goal.

DANNY: So I know you're there. I just don't want to look.

(MARK nods. He starts the car. The radio comes on by itself, loud, a song neither of them likes. Neither of them turns it off.)

MARK: Maccas?

DANNY: (after a moment) Yeah.

(MARK pulls out. As the car turns, DANNY reaches over and turns the radio down, just a little. MARK lets him. Lights fade.)

The ending resolves the immediate conflict through a small, mutual compromise, but it leaves the deeper pattern of inherited pressure only partly addressed, which makes it a convincing rather than a neat resolution.

The turning point is Danny's request: "Next time can you stand somewhere I can't see you?" The stage direction "It lands" signals its force, and Mark's gesture of taking "his hands off the wheel" and putting them "in his lap" symbolically surrenders control. His reply, "Yeah, mate. I can do that", is plain but sincere, marking a genuine shift.

Danny's clarification is crucial to the emotional balance: "So I know you're there. I just don't want to look." The line distinguishes presence from pressure, reassuring Mark that he is wanted while setting a boundary. This reframes Mark's anecdote about his own absent father; the son does not want the absence Mark suffered, only some distance. The cycle is adjusted rather than repeated.

The loud song "neither of them likes" is left playing, since "Neither of them turns it off", suggesting a shared, tolerant discomfort, and the brief exchange "Maccas?" and "Yeah." restores ordinary routine. Most tellingly, Danny turns the radio down "just a little" and "MARK lets him", mirroring the opening seatbelt moment but reversing it: now the son acts and the father allows.

However, the playwright does not resolve everything. Mark's question "Do you?" is never answered, and his need to be present remains. The ending is effective because it resolves the scene's conflict in a modest, believable way while acknowledging that the relationship will keep negotiating its distance.

sets.title: The Housekeeper, to the New Girl
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original dramatic monologue written in an older style. It is set in a wealthy Sydney household in the 1880s; the speaker is a fictional housekeeper addressing a newly hired maid. A 'character' was a written reference from a former employer; the 'copper' was a large boiler used for washing clothes.
sets.body:
Mind how you set the tray, girl. Silver first,
then china, then yourself, and last of all
your opinions, which in this house are kept
like spoons that are not ours to use. Sit down.
You'll not sit often here, so learn it now.

The mistress rings at seven. Not before.
You'll know her bell; it has a peevish note,
as if the house had wronged it in the night.
The master takes his tea at eight, alone,
and reads the shipping news aloud to no one.
You'll answer when he speaks. He does not speak.

The girl before you? Bridget. Clever hands.
She dressed the mistress's hair as if it mattered,
and sang at the copper, which I let her do,
for there's no rule against a song, God knows,
though there is one against its being heard.
A brooch was lost in March. A garnet brooch.
The mistress turned the house out like a drawer
and found it nowhere, and found Bridget handy.
They sent her off without a character.
You'll know what that means soon enough, I'd wager.

The young master came home that week from town
with a new watch-chain and a careless laugh.
I keep the linen. I keep the household books.
I keep my counsel, which is the hardest keeping.
Don't look at me like that. Pour out the tea.

You'll do. You're quiet. Quiet girls do well.
And if you hear the copper singing, girl,
on wash-days, when the steam is thick and low,
you'll tell yourself it's only water boiling.

Her ordered list, "Silver first, / then china, then yourself", places the girl below the objects she serves, and "last of all / your opinions" ranks her inner life lowest. The simile comparing opinions to "spoons that are not ours to use" implies that a servant's thoughts effectively belong to her employers, to be kept but never used. Even the command "Sit down" is undercut by the warning "You'll not sit often here", showing that rest, like opinion, is a rare privilege. The brisk imperatives present a woman who has internalised the hierarchy and now enforces it.

questions.model: The poet uses juxtaposition, implication and the speaker's guarded tone to suggest that the young master, not Bridget, took the brooch, and that the housekeeper knows it. The accusation against Bridget is framed sardonically: the mistress "found it nowhere, and found Bridget handy", where the repetition of "found" exposes the injustice of choosing a convenient scapegoat. The stanza break then places a seemingly unrelated detail directly after Bridget's dismissal: the young master returned "with a new watch-chain and a careless laugh". The speaker never states a connection, but the juxtaposition invites the reader to infer that the garnet brooch paid for the chain, and "careless" implies his indifference to the harm caused. The anaphora of "I keep the linen. I keep the household books." reveals that the housekeeper has access to the accounts and therefore to knowledge, while the climactic "I keep my counsel, which is the hardest keeping" confesses the moral cost of her silence. Her sudden command "Don't look at me like that" suggests the new girl has understood, signalling to the reader that the inference is correct. The poem makes its accusation entirely through implication.

questions.model:
The poem invites considerable but qualified sympathy for the housekeeper: she is complicit in an unjust household, yet the dramatic monologue lets the reader hear the cost of that complicity, so she emerges as both an agent and a casualty of the hierarchy she enforces.

The case against her is clear. She trains the new girl in self-erasure, ranking "yourself" below silver and china, and she knew that Bridget was dismissed "without a character" yet did nothing. Her remark "You'll know what that means soon enough, I'd wager" carries a hint of threat, and the closing instruction that the girl should tell herself "it's only water boiling" asks her to adopt the same willed blindness. In this sense the housekeeper perpetuates injustice.

However, the poet repeatedly signals that her hardness is a survival strategy shaped by powerlessness. The mistress's bell with "a peevish note, / as if the house had wronged it" and the master who "does not speak" depict employers who are petty and indifferent, which places the speaker's coldness in context. Her memory of Bridget is tender, "Clever hands", and she recalls the girl who "sang at the copper, which I let her do". The aside "there's no rule against a song, God knows, / though there is one against its being heard" is bitterly ironic, revealing her awareness that servants may have inner lives only if they remain unheard.

The strongest source of sympathy is her confession that keeping "my counsel" is "the hardest keeping". The phrase concedes a guilt she cannot act upon, and the closing image of the copper "singing" on wash-days suggests she is haunted by Bridget's absence. The steam "thick and low" obscures sight, mirroring the moral fog in which she lives.

Ultimately, the dramatic monologue form makes sympathy hard to withhold, because the speaker exposes more of her conscience than she intends. She is not innocent, but the poem suggests her silence is the product of a system that punishes speech, so the reader judges the household more harshly than the woman who serves it.

sets.title: In Defence of Boredom
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original personal essay. The writer is fictional.
sets.body:
When I was nine, the most boring place in the world was my grandmother's lounge room in Launceston on a Sunday afternoon. There was a clock that ticked as if it were being paid by the tick. There was a bowl of wax fruit nobody was allowed to touch. There was a television, but it lived under a crocheted cover, like a budgie that had been put to bed. And there was me, on the carpet, with nothing to do for three hours while the adults talked about people who had died.

I want to say clearly, before I go on, that I hated it. I am not one of those people who looks back on childhood suffering and calls it character. I was bored to the point of physical pain. I counted the squares in the carpet pattern. I tried to read the newspaper upside down. I lay on my back and stared at the ceiling until the light fitting began to look like a jellyfish, and then like a face, and then like a map of an island that does not exist, which I named and populated and governed, with some cruelty, for the rest of the afternoon.

That island, it turns out, is the reason I am a writer.

I have been thinking about this because I have not been bored, properly bored, in perhaps eleven years. I have a phone. You have a phone. Between us we have abolished the waiting room, the bus stop, the queue at the bank, the ten minutes before a film starts. Every gap in the day now has something in it, the way every gap in a cheap wall has filler. I can no longer remember the last time I stared at a ceiling long enough for it to become anything other than a ceiling.

The usual way to argue this is with research, and there is research, though I am suspicious of anyone who tells you that a study has proved something about your soul. So let me argue it the other way, from the carpet. Boredom is not empty. Boredom is the feeling of your mind discovering that nobody is going to entertain it, and deciding, slowly and resentfully, to entertain itself. It is the dull grey waiting room outside imagination. You cannot get into the room without sitting in the waiting room first.

I do not want to romanticise this. Boredom is also what happens to people in jobs that grind them down, in hospitals, in detention, in lives with no doors in them. That boredom is not a gift. It is a wound, and nobody should be told to be grateful for it. The boredom I am defending is a smaller and more privileged thing: the bored afternoon that has an end.

But I think it is worth defending. Last month, on a delayed train, my phone died. For forty minutes I looked out of the window at the backs of houses, their washing lines and trampolines and bins. Around the twentieth minute, something unlocked. I began to wonder about the people who lived there, and then to invent them, and by the time the train moved I had the first page of a story.

My grandmother's clock is in my hallway now. It still ticks as if it is being paid by the tick. I have never once wanted to throw it out.

questions.model:
The writer's tone moves from comic nostalgia to reflective argument, then to sober qualification and finally to quiet affirmation, and each shift strengthens the credibility of the defence of boredom.

The opening is playful. Hyperbole and simile, such as the clock that ticked "as if it were being paid by the tick" and the television under its cover "like a budgie that had been put to bed", make the grandmother's lounge room comically lifeless, so the reader shares the child's suffering. The writer then insists "that I hated it", refusing to sentimentalise; this honesty earns trust before the argument begins.

The one-line paragraph "That island, it turns out, is the reason I am a writer" shifts the tone to revelation. The following paragraph adopts a direct, inclusive register: "I have a phone. You have a phone." The parallel sentences implicate the reader, and the comparison with filler in "every gap in a cheap wall" makes constant stimulation seem shoddy.

The most significant shift is to seriousness: "I do not want to romanticise this." Here the writer acknowledges boredom in "detention" and in "lives with no doors in them", calling it "a wound". This sober concession limits the claim to "the bored afternoon that has an end", making the argument more precise and harder to dismiss.

The ending returns to a gentle, warm tone. The clock that still ticks "as if it is being paid by the tick" echoes the opening, but now with affection: "I have never once wanted to throw it out." The circular return shows the writer's attitude transformed, embodying the argument that boredom, remembered, becomes valuable.

questions.model:
I find the writer's defence of boredom largely convincing, because it argues from vivid personal evidence, defines its terms honestly and anticipates the strongest objection. Its persuasiveness is limited, however, by its reliance on a single kind of experience, which the writer openly admits is privileged.

The essay's greatest strength is that it shows rather than asserts the process it defends. The account of staring at the ceiling until the light fitting looked "like a jellyfish, and then like a face, and then like a map of an island that does not exist" enacts the movement from boredom to invention; the cumulative structure lets the reader watch imagination arrive. When the writer then claims, "That island, it turns out, is the reason I am a writer", the conclusion feels earned.

The writer is also convincing in redefining boredom precisely. Rather than "empty", it is "the feeling of your mind discovering that nobody is going to entertain it", and the metaphor of "the dull grey waiting room outside imagination" captures both its discomfort and its purpose. The claim that "You cannot get into the room without sitting in the waiting room first" is memorable, though it is an assertion rather than a demonstrated truth.

The handling of counter-arguments adds credibility. The writer is wary of research that claims to have "proved something about your soul", choosing to argue "from the carpet", which some readers may see as evasive. More persuasively, the writer concedes that for people in grinding jobs or "detention" boredom "is a wound", limiting the case to "the bored afternoon that has an end". This honesty prevents the essay from sounding glib.

The weakness is that the evidence is anecdotal and comes from a writer, someone predisposed to value imaginative drift. The train anecdote, in which the "first page of a story" arrives after forty minutes, may not persuade a reader who simply finds boredom unpleasant.

Overall, I find the essay convincing as a reflective argument rather than a proof: its candour, imagery and careful limits make a modest claim persuasively, even if they cannot make a universal one.

sets.title: The Last Milk Bar on Ferris Street
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original feature article. The people, the shop and the suburb are fictional.
sets.body:
At 6.15 every morning, Eleni Kostas turns the sign on the door of the Ferris Street Milk Bar from CLOSED to OPEN, and then, because the hinge is loose, she turns it back again with her thumb so it stays straight. She has done this for forty-three years. 'The sign is older than my son,' she says. 'It complains more, too.'

The milk bar sits on the corner of Ferris and Dunn streets, in a suburb that has changed around it like water around a stone. The fruit shop is now a pilates studio. The bank is a café that serves coffee in jars. Across the road, a supermarket with self-service lanes and a car park the size of a football field opened six years ago. And still, every morning, a small queue forms outside Eleni's door: tradies wanting pies, schoolkids wanting mixed lollies, an elderly man who wants nothing but the newspaper and ten minutes of conversation about the football.

Milk bars were once everywhere in Australian suburbs, many of them run by migrant families, Greek and Italian especially, who worked long hours behind counters stacked with sweets and magazines. Most have now closed. Eleni knows she is something of a survivor. She does not seem to find it romantic.

'People come in and take photos,' she says, wiping down a counter that is already clean. 'They say, oh, it's so nostalgic. Then they go and buy their milk at the supermarket.' She shrugs. 'Nostalgia doesn't pay the electricity.'

Her husband, Kostas, died fifteen years ago. (Yes, she says, laughing, she married a man whose first name was her surname. 'Everybody in the village thought it was very efficient.') Since then she has run the shop alone, with occasional help from her granddaughter, Sofia, who is nineteen and studying engineering.

Sofia has opinions about the business. She has set up a card machine, an Instagram account and a spreadsheet. 'Yiayia's system was a notebook,' she says. 'Which was actually incredible. She knew every customer's tab to the cent. But you can't sell a notebook.'

Is she going to take over? Sofia laughs, then stops laughing. 'I don't know,' she says. 'I love it. But I don't want to love it the way she loves it. She hasn't had a holiday since 1994.'

What keeps people coming back is difficult to measure. Tom Le, a plumber who has stopped here every working day for a decade, struggles to explain. 'The pies are fine,' he says. 'They're not the best pies.' He thinks. 'She asked about my daughter when she was sick. Every day. Even after she was better, Eleni still asked. You don't get that at the servo.'

At closing time, Eleni counts the till by hand, though the card machine has already done it for her. She saves the coins in a biscuit tin for her grandchildren. When I ask what will happen to the shop when she retires, she looks at me as if I have asked something faintly rude.

'Retire,' she says, trying the word like an unfamiliar sweet. Then she turns the sign. It swings crooked. She leaves it.

questions.model:
The article suggests that as suburbs change, communities gain convenience and novelty but risk losing the personal attention and continuity that small businesses provide; yet it also implies that what is valuable can be partly carried forward, in a new form, by the next generation.

The central image of the suburb that "has changed around it like water around a stone" frames the milk bar as a fixed point amid gentrification. The list of replacements, the fruit shop now "a pilates studio" and the bank "a café that serves coffee in jars", is gently satirical, implying that newer businesses cater to lifestyle rather than daily need. The supermarket with "a car park the size of a football field" represents scale and efficiency, against which the "small queue" outside Eleni's shop seems fragile but loyal.

What is lost, the article suggests, is relationship. Tom Le's comment "You don't get that at the servo" identifies personal care as the milk bar's real product, something "difficult to measure", and Eleni's notebook, in which she "knew every customer's tab to the cent", represents a form of knowledge built on trust.

However, the article resists simple nostalgia. Eleni's dry remark that "Nostalgia doesn't pay the electricity" warns that sentiment alone cannot sustain such places, while Sofia's card machine, "Instagram account and a spreadsheet" show adaptation is possible. Sofia's ambivalence, "I don't want to love it the way she loves it", suggests the next generation may keep the values without the self-sacrifice.

The final image of the sign that "swings crooked" and is left that way draws these ideas together: imperfection and change are accepted, but for now the shop stays open.
